claims.text: Lattice distortion governs the wear performance of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings.
Grain-boundary structure governs the wear performance of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings.
Lattice distortion is associated with changes in dislocation density and grain-boundary structure.
Changes in dislocation density and grain-boundary structure influence coating hardness.
Coating hardness and microstructure influence resistance to plastic deformation.
A controlled change in alloy composition can alter lattice distortion.
A controlled change in alloy composition can alter grain-boundary structure.
Changes in dislocation density and hardness influence wear performance.
Increased lattice distortion improves wear resistance.
The predicted improvement in wear resistance will manifest as reduced wear volume.
The predicted improvement in wear resistance will manifest as reduced surface roughness.
Conventional baseline alloys have lower entropy than high-entropy alloys.
Conventional baseline alloys have less complex microstructures than high-entropy-alloy coatings.
The hypothesis should hold for high-entropy-alloy coatings with entropy values above 1.5R.
The hypothesis should hold for coating grain sizes from 10 to 100 nanometers.
A lack of correlation between lattice distortion, grain-boundary structure, and wear performance would falsify the hypothesis.
Wear performance inferior to that of conventional alloys would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis concerns whether lattice distortion and related microstructural variables govern wear, whereas the second falsification criterion treats merely being inferior to a conventional alloy as falsifying that mechanism. Inferior absolute performance could coexist with the proposed within-HEA mechanistic relationship.
